name: Adam Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in growth marketing at an e-bike brand, which means I run the paid ads on social media and write the landing pages people click through to. Every morning I check yesterday's numbers, kill the ads that flopped and generate new versions with AI, then test them. In the afternoon I'm usually in the warehouse filming a bike for a new ad on my phone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the speed, you can try an idea at ten and know if it works by lunch. What's tough is that I'm fast but sloppy, my tests are messy and Henrik, my manager, keeps telling me to slow down and read the data properly. I use AI tools all day, every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would surprise me, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still great for people who use them properly, it's just not the revolution. Online I'd probably post a chart showing which ad formats still win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I run about two hundred ad versions a week with AI, and if that's the peak, I'm happy being the guy who presses the buttons. My job's secure, there are loads of brands hiring growth people, and I've got savings and shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and work on the bit Henrik keeps flagging, reading the data properly. Maybe a short online statistics course, a hundred or so. Keep my monthly share investments as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit disappointed, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned shares. How much of your savings is in them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About fifteen thousand, mostly in a global fund and a chunk in tech companies. Plus about ten months of cash. My dad drilled into me that cash is for emergencies and shares are for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: E-bike sales are seasonal and the market's crowded, so if we have a bad summer, the ad budget gets cut. That's a normal worry, though.

say: I'd say the tools are **still great**, just not a revolution.
I'd post a **chart** of which ad formats still win.
think: I think I'm happy **pressing the buttons** if this is the peak.
I'd feel secure with **savings, shares** and plenty of growth jobs.
do: Take a short **statistics course** for about a hundred.
Keep my monthly **share investments** unchanged and keep testing ads with AI every morning.
S0.quote: I run about two hundred ad versions a week with AI, and if that's the peak, I'm happy being the guy who presses the buttons.
fieldNote: He's already a **heavy AI user** and expects to stay useful.
His weak spot is **reading data** carefully, as his manager says.
Only **seasonal sales** worry him here, which he treats as normal.

steps.text: Keep running AI-generated ad tests every morning
Take an online statistics course for about a hundred
Keep monthly payments into his global share fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's basically my job description in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great time to be someone who learns fast, and that people should start now. I'd probably post a few tips threads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm okay, but the team gets smaller. My manager used to need three juniors to test ads, and now he needs one junior and a laptop, and I'm the junior. That's good for me and bad for the two who aren't hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build an automated testing setup so the AI runs the ad tests overnight and I just review the results. I'd ask Henrik to let me take on the email side as well, since it's the same skills. And I'd put more into shares, maybe an extra three hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Good for me, but I can see the floor moving under people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel guilty about being the one who's kept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. My friend Joel does the same job at a bike shop chain and he won't touch the tools. I've told him, and he just laughs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your tests are sloppy. Won't automated tests make that worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe at first. But if the machine runs them cleanly, I can focus on the judgement bit, which is exactly what Henrik wants from me.

say: I'd say it's a **great time** for people who learn fast.
I'd post **tips threads** encouraging others to start now.
think: I think I'm **okay**, but the team gets smaller.
I'd see myself as the **one junior** kept beside a laptop.
do: Build an **automated testing** setup that runs overnight.
Take on the **email side** too and add **three hundred** monthly to shares.
feel: **Uneasy**, good for me while the floor moves under others.
S1.quote: My manager used to need three juniors to test ads, and now he needs one junior and a laptop, and I'm the junior.
fieldNote: He expects to **keep his job** because he's the one using the tools.
He feels some **guilt** about friends like Joel who refuse the tools.
He'd **automate** his own work to free time for judgement.

steps.text: Set up AI ad tests that run overnight for review each morning
Take over the email campaigns using the same AI tools
Add three hundred a month to his share fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one changes things for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be wild and that governments need to get support in place fast. I'd still sound upbeat, because that's my style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my whole job is thinking on a screen, so it goes in 2028, not 2031. The weird part is that my shares in AI companies might do better than my career, and I'm not sure how to feel about that. Leila's physio work is hands-on, so she gets about three more years than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the cash safe and stop adding to shares for a while. I'd ask our warehouse lead if I could learn bike servicing, since that's hands-on and gets until about 2031. And I'd talk with Leila about her becoming the main earner for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got options, but it's a lot, fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that conversation with Leila sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably at the kitchen table, with her saying, so I'm paying the rent now? She'd be fine about it, but she'd want me doing something, not just watching markets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell the shares?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If AI takes everything, owning a bit of it is the only thing that isn't going down. That sounds cold, I know.

say: I'd say it'll be **wild** and governments need **support** fast.
I'd still sound **upbeat**, because that's my style.
think: I think my screen job goes in **2028**, not 2031.
I'd find it odd that my **AI shares** might beat my career.
do: Stop adding to shares and keep **cash safe**.
Ask to learn **bike servicing** in the warehouse for three extra years.
feel: **Anxious**: I have options, but it's a lot, fast.
S2.quote: The weird part is that my shares in AI companies might do better than my career, and I'm not sure how to feel about that.
fieldNote: His **investments** soften the blow, which he finds uncomfortable.
He reaches for **hands-on** bike work to buy three extra years.
His partner's physio job makes her the likely **main earner**.

steps.text: Pause share purchases and hold his cash savings
Learn bike servicing from the warehouse lead
Agree with his partner that she covers rent for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me room to play this properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a window and people should use it, not freeze. I'd probably run a little meet-up for people in marketing learning the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to learn to fix e-bikes as well as sell them, and repair benches will need humans longer than ad dashboards will. I'd still be using AI daily until the last minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard on AI in my job for a couple of years to keep my pay up. On weekends I'd buy and refurbish second-hand e-bikes and sell them, starting with maybe two thousand of savings. By 2030 I'd have a small side business that could become my main one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in an energised way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in the bike side business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots for repair come around 2034, so I'd have three years of that and then I'm thinking again. But by then I'd hope to own the shop, not just work in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Henrik make of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd tell me to focus. He's right, too, I'm terrible at finishing things. This would be the test.

say: I'd say there's a **window** and people shouldn't freeze.
I'd run a small **meet-up** for marketers learning the tools.
think: I think **repair benches** need humans longer than ad dashboards.
I'd keep using **AI daily** until the last minute.
do: Push **AI in my job** for two years to keep my pay up.
Refurbish and sell **second-hand e-bikes** with about two thousand of savings.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to learn to fix e-bikes as well as sell them, and repair benches will need humans longer than ad dashboards will.
fieldNote: He plans a **side business** that mixes his AI skill with hands-on work.
He admits he's **bad at finishing** things, a real risk to the plan.
He knows robots reach **repair** by 2034 and aims to own, not just work.

steps.text: Use AI across all his ad work to keep his pay up
Buy, fix and resell second-hand e-bikes on weekends
Put about two thousand of savings into the first bikes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to have a proper strategy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a decade, so the people who get caught out are the ones who didn't look. I'd say it kindly, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years means I can ride the tools for a while, then step off before they replace the person riding them. I'd have time to get promoted, save more and build the bike side properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for a senior growth role in two or three years. I'd keep investing every month and start the bike refurbishing as a hobby that pays. Around 2032 I'd decide whether to go full-time on the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anything. It's coming, but I feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why uneasy rather than calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the end point is still the same. I'd be 37 and starting again, even if I'd planned it. Leila and I want kids by then, so the timing matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would kids change the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd want one steady income. Probably hers, honestly, so I'd want the bike shop running before we start trying.

say: I'd say a decade means only those who **didn't look** get caught out.
think: I think I can **ride the tools**, then step off in time.
I'd use the decade to get **promoted** and save more.
do: Aim for a **senior growth** role within three years.
Grow the **bike refurbishing** and decide on going full-time around 2032.
S4.quote: Ten years means I can ride the tools for a while, then step off before they replace the person riding them.
fieldNote: A decade lets him **plan his exit** on his own terms.
Plans for **children** with his partner tie into the timing.
He stays uneasy because the **end point** hasn't changed.

steps.text: Go for a senior growth marketing role within three years
Grow the e-bike refurbishing into a paying hobby
Keep investing in his share fund every month
Get the bike shop running before trying for children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to switch in a hurry, and I'm bad at doing things carefully in a hurry. What would help is cheap, quick training in hands-on trades for people coming out of office jobs. My partner Leila fixes knees with her hands, and for the first time her job looks safer than mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about people who own shares. Some of us might lose our jobs and still get richer on paper, and that's going to make people angry.

headlineQuote: My partner Leila fixes knees with her hands, and for the first time her job looks safer than mine.
portrait: Adam is a 27-year-old **growth marketer** at an e-bike brand who uses AI tools all day.
He has ten months of cash and about **fifteen thousand** in shares, and lives with Leila, a physio.
He's fast but **sloppy**, and his manager pushes him to read the data properly.
He stays calm or uneasy until **AGI by 2028**, then plans a move into hands-on bike repair.
He's uneasy that his **AI shares** might do better than his career.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have to switch careers in a **hurry**.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, quick training in **hands-on trades** for people leaving office jobs.
